title: Occasions of writing do not cancel the divine mandate to write
source_text: XIII. Frustra quoque notat Bellarminus varias occasiones quibus ad scribendum invitati fuerunt Apostoli & Evangelistae. Matthaeum, exempli gratia, Evangelium scripsisse ut Hebraeis, quos deserebat ad Gentes proficiscens, aliquod memoriale doctrinae & praedicationis suae relinqueret. Johannem vero suum Evangelium edidisse rogantibus Asiae Episcopis, propter Ebionitarum haeresim tunc exorientem. Lucam vero aggressum fuisse Evangelicam historiam scribere, ut nos abstraheret ab incertis aliorum narrationibus. Unde colligit Bellarminus Apostolos & Evangelistas obiter tantum scripsisse, & per occasionem, non vero quasi ex proprio munere & divino mandato. Sed quamvis scriptoribus sacris variae occasiones scribendi oblatae fuerint, non ideo tamen absque mandato divino scripserunt. Fuerunt enim a Deo inspirati, quod fortissimum mandati genus est, ut arriperent illas occasiones doctrinam sacram scripto consignandi ad perpetuum Ecclesiae usum, non vero simpliciter ut singulari cuipiam incommodo mederentur.
pass_a_gloss: In vain too does Bellarmine note the various occasions by which the Apostles and Evangelists were invited to write. Matthew, for example, wrote a Gospel so that to the Hebrews whom he was leaving as he set out to the Gentiles he might leave some memorial of his doctrine and preaching. John published his Gospel at the request of the bishops of Asia, because of the Ebionite heresy then arising. Luke undertook to write the Evangelical history to draw us away from uncertain narrations of others. From this Bellarmine gathers that the Apostles and Evangelists wrote only in passing and by occasion, not as from their proper office and a divine mandate. But although various occasions of writing were offered to the sacred writers, they did not therefore write without a divine mandate. For they were inspired by God — the strongest kind of mandate — to seize those occasions of consigning sacred doctrine to writing for the perpetual use of the Church, not merely to remedy some particular person's inconvenience.
pass_b_english: Bellarmine lists occasions: Matthew's memorial, John's anti-Ebionite request, Luke vs uncertain tales.
He infers they wrote casually, not by office or divine order.
Occasions do not cancel mandate — inspiration is the strongest mandate of all.
They seized those occasions for the Church's perpetual use, not for one private fix.

lemmas.gloss: only in passing and by occasion
